anchors.fact: He taught English at a Los Angeles high school, and after a 1970 trip wanted to live in Amsterdam, a place where, in his words, he "could really learn a lot about myself", but he didn't know how a public-school teacher could (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; Oxford Companion pdf 2260; *Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: A safe job, and a wish to be somewhere else with no plan yet.

anchors.fact: He worked out the how on a road trip through Mexico: open something the city lacked, Mexican food. "My main goal was to support myself," he said (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; *Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: The reason was small and plain: a way to live where he wanted, on his own pay.

anchors.fact: In 1976 he opened Café Pacifico in Amsterdam with little money, on a street where people told him they'd never come because it was "too dangerous"; within six weeks there were queues, as his partner Phil Bayly remembered (*A Proper Drink* p. 79; Oxford pdf 743; Bayly, CLASS, 2021). He had never been a bartender or a cook (his own account, via Bayly).
anchors.meaning: Starting from nothing, with what was on the record: no money, no trade.

anchors.fact: His partner's account of his rule for the staff: "Tight on bottom, loose on top": do the job well, and you could do it in your own style (Bayly, CLASS, 2021).
anchors.meaning: The freedom he left to find, he handed to the people who worked for him.

anchors.fact: In London (from 1982) young bartenders "having few places to go" found Pacifico, and Danny Smith spent ten years there making Margaritas for bartenders off their shifts (*A Proper Drink* pp. 79–80, 98). At La Perla, another of his London places, Dre Masso, a bartender Danny Smith brought along one night, told Smith "I felt like I was at home" (p. 80).
anchors.meaning: What he built for himself became where others belonged, in their words, not his.

anchors.fact: In 2017 he said he was handing his shares in London's Pacifico to the people who worked there, "a cooperative", keeping a minority stake because he wanted "to still be a bar owner – and be part of the community" (*Drinks International*, 2017).
anchors.meaning: He wanted to stay in it as one of them, not over them. (His words in 2017; how the handover ended isn't on record. His regret in the same answer, that he should have got out of the way about five years sooner, is used in y3 and y5; "ashamed" stays in the dossier.)

anchors.fact: Pacifico's Margaritas were made with Sauza Blanco and Giffard triple sec, "to Estes' specifications", according to Danny Smith (*A Proper Drink* p. 79); Estes's proportions aren't on record, so ours are the *Cocktail Codex*'s classic (p. 166). The Margarita is one of the drinks that have "indisputably achieved" classic status (Oxford Companion, CLASSIC COCKTAIL, pdf 473). Today's basic Sauza silver is a mixto (51% agave; Oxford SAUZA pdf 1743), and Giffard sells a 25% and a 40% triple sec. Ours are Sauza's 100% agave blanco and Giffard's 25% Triple Sec: his brands, not necessarily his bottlings.
anchors.meaning: The measured half of the glass is his half: the brands he chose, kept exact. The top is left to whoever makes it, as his partner remembered his rule.

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the bottom exactly. Then hand the top to someone else, and join the people you made room for.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 200 ml), chilled, no salt
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you work.
Measure the tequila, triple sec, lime juice and syrup into a shaker. Measure them exactly: this is the tight part.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold comfortably.
Empty the glass and strain the drink into it. No salt.

Now the loose part. Cut a wide strip of grapefruit peel with as little white as you can, hold it skin-side down over the glass and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink, then rest it on the rim. That's my top. If someone else is making it, the top is theirs: anything that goes on the drink rather than into it.
cocktail.name: Loose on Top

cocktail.tagline: You never wanted to be the boss. You just couldn't bear having one.

reading.epigraph: One restaurant owner chose the brands in this drink. Whoever's pouring chooses the top.
whoYouAre: You started something of your own. Maybe a Sunday football team, a stall at the weekend market, a supper that turned into a monthly thing, or a whole business. When people ask why, they expect a big reason. The real one is smaller, and you rarely say it: you wanted to live your way, and pay your own way doing it.

There's something else you keep quiet. Somewhere along the line, other people started treating it as theirs. They turn up early, bring friends and save each other seats. And part of you worries about ending up in the corner, keeping the whole thing running for everyone else to belong to. The freedom you went out for always turns out to have room for other people in it.
yours: Tomas Estes taught English in Los Angeles and wanted to live in Amsterdam, a place where, he said, he could learn a lot about himself. He couldn't see how a teacher could manage it. A Mexican restaurant could. "My main goal was to support myself," he said, though one writer saw it differently: the restaurant was his way to freedom.

He opened Café Pacifico there in 1976, with little money, on a street people told him was too dangerous to visit. A second Pacifico opened in London, around a long bar. Young bartenders with few places to go for a proper cocktail found it, and one of its barmen spent ten years making Margaritas for the ones just off their shifts. At another of his London places, one bartender said he felt at home.

His partner Phil Bayly remembered his rule for the staff: "Tight on bottom, loose on top." Get the work right, then do it your way. I like to think that's the whole of him: he left to be free, then gave the same freedom away. In 2017 he said he was handing his shares in the London restaurant to the partners who worked there, keeping a minority share because he wanted to stay "part of the community". He added that he should probably have got out of the way five years sooner.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Margarita, a renowned classic. I made it with the two brands one of his London barmen said Estes chose, Sauza for the tequila and Giffard for the triple sec, shaken hard with fresh lime and served ice-cold, with no salt. The bottom is measured to the drop, as a nod to the tight half of his rule. The top is the loose half: I squeeze the oils of a grapefruit peel over it, and when someone else makes it, the top is theirs to choose. It only ever goes on the drink, never into it, so whatever they pick, the drink underneath still holds.

Don't leave it as late as he did. Whatever you've started, the team, the stall, the thing with your name on the door, hand someone the piece you've kept hold of and let them do it their way. It won't be how you'd do it. It'll be theirs, and that means it's working. Then turn up the way everyone else does: early, with a friend, for no reason except that you like it there. You went out on your own to be free. You don't have to stay on your own to keep it.
